title: Thermodynamic Measure of Intelligence
abstract: Can intelligence be measured? We propose that intelligence can be defined as the lawful amplification of rare but valid futures: a system increases the probability of outcomes that would be unlikely under passive dynamics but remain admissible under the constraints of the domain. We start with the premise that an intelligent system must model the world and its own place within it. Because the system is part of the world it models, this leads naturally to recursive self-simulation: the system represents futures in which its own actions are part of the trajectory. Our central results give a necessity statement and a conditional near-sufficiency statement connecting this architecture to a precise thermodynamic measure of lawful amplification of rare-valid futures: high rare-valid lift is impossible unless the internal simulation identifies rare-valid futures with high fidelity; conversely, when rare-valid fidelity is high and the simulation contains an effective policy, the achievable lift approaches the actuation-limited optimum. Thus recursive self-simulation is not merely a plausible feature of intelligence but, under the stated assumptions, is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence. The resulting framework makes intelligence measurable on a universal scale, from passive matter and feedback controllers, large language models, and humans as text generators to Maxwell-demon-like information engines.
summary: This work proposes a universal thermodynamic measure of intelligence based on how an agent amplifies the probability of rare but physically valid futures. It mathematically links this amplification ('rare-valid lift') directly to the necessity of recursive self-simulation within the agent's internal model. The framework provides quantitative metrics applicable across diverse systems, from classical controllers to advanced AI models.
main_problem: To define and measure intelligence as a physical, thermodynamic quantity by quantifying its ability to amplify rare but valid futures.
main_result: Recursive self-simulation is necessary and nearly sufficient for high thermodynamic intelligence, which is quantified by the 'rare-valid lift' relative to passive dynamics.
method: The framework uses non-equilibrium fluctuation theorems and information theory to compare induced path laws ($P$) against a passive baseline law ($P_0$).
model_or_system: The model involves abstract systems ranging from passive matter and feedback controllers to LLMs, analyzed via their ability to generate or select rare trajectories in the space of possible futures.
key_observables: Rare-valid lift ($\mathcal{I}_\delta$), Path-deviation divergence ($	ext{DKL}$), and the stabilized double-log scale ($\Lambda$).
important_parameters: The measure is highly dependent on specified parameters: baseline law, validity criterion, level of description, and trajectory resolution.
main_assumptions: Assumes applicability of fluctuation theorems; requires explicit definition of baselines and validity sets for measurement to be meaningful.
figures_summary: Figures conceptually illustrate recursive self-simulation across modeling levels and define the thermodynamic intelligence measure ($\mathcal{I}_\delta$) as a lift relative to passive dynamics.
paper_structure: The paper builds from defining intelligence via rare-valid amplification, establishing mathematical links between this concept and simulation fidelity (Theorems 1 & 2), deriving bounds using path deviation measures (Theorem 3), and finally applying the framework to symbolic generation and physical engines.
why_interesting: While not directly about quantum systems, the use of fluctuation theorems and information geometry provides powerful mathematical tools for analyzing non-equilibrium processes, which are central to open quantum system dynamics and measurement theory.
